reading.body:
CyrusOne's Quincy facility publishes 36 megawatts of IT capacity, making it the largest announced capacity data center in Washington state and representing 60 percent of the state's total published power.

This concentration matters because AI training is power-constrained, and Washington has only two data centers with public capacity figures despite 46 mapped facilities statewide. The Quincy site's 36 megawatts, translating to roughly 900 racks at typical AI training density, sits in Grant County near hydroelectric resources from the Columbia River system. Yet the actual grid connection and power sourcing remain unpublished, leaving unclear whether this facility's proximity to abundant generation translates to actual access or whether it competes for existing transmission capacity.

The data shows what is announced but not what is built or expanding. No certifications are published, and no expansion plans appear in the record. Of Washington's 46 data center locations, 44 publish no power figure at all, suggesting either much smaller scale, operational status still in planning, or intentional opacity. The state's total announced capacity of 60 megawatts is negligible compared to regions already saturated with hyperscale infrastructure, indicating either nascent development or that most capacity remains undeclared.
